lines: Imagine falling from the sky through a violent storm and waking up alone in a deadly jungle.
On 24 December 1971 a passenger plane is struck by lightning and breaks apart midair.
Seventeen year old Juliane Koepcke falls about 3000 meters while still strapped to her seat row.
She wakes up on the dark forest floor with a broken collarbone and a deep arm cut.
She also suffers from a painful eye injury and a severe concussion after the terrifying plunge.
Her biologist father previously taught her that following flowing water always leads back to people.
She finds a tiny creek and begins walking through the dense and dangerous Peruvian rainforest.
Days pass slowly as she follows the winding water toward a larger and safer river.
Up to 14 other passengers survive the initial crash but tragically die before any rescue arrives.
She spends 11 long days completely alone in the unforgiving jungle facing unimaginable odds.
After 9 days of difficult travel she finally discovers a remote lumberjack camp by the river.
She is found by local workers who provide medical help and bring her back to safety.
Juliane remains the only official survivor of LANSA Flight 508 against all odds and expectations.
Would you have the mental strength to survive 11 days alone in the dangerous rainforest?

lines: If an avalanche catches you on a slope, do not try to outrun the moving snow.
Jake has less than 15 minutes to survive when the mountain slope suddenly breaks apart.
A massive slab of heavy snow crashes down the peak, rushing straight toward his shelter.
One. Try to get off the sliding slab to the side as it starts moving.
Jake scrambles toward a rock overhang, but the fast white wave sweeps him away.
Two. If you are swept away, fight with swimming motions to stay on top.
He swims against the crushing current and dumps his heavy pack to avoid sinking down.
Three. As the snow slows, cup your arm in front of your face quickly.
Jake crouches down beneath the rock overhang and creates a crucial air pocket around his face.
He pushes one hand up toward the surface right as the debris comes to a stop.
Jake waves his bare hand through the top crust to show rescuers where he is buried.
Most buried people need to be dug out within about 15 minutes to stay alive.
Essential rescue gear like a beacon, probe, and shovel can save a life in time.
Jake secured his breathing space and marked his exact location for his waiting climbing partner.
It was the perfect plan for survival. There was just one major problem left.
The heavy snow is packing tight, and his partner has no shovel to dig him out.
part1.cliffhanger: Jake is buried under heavy snow with an air pocket, but his partner lacks a shovel to dig him out before his 15 minutes run out.
